choices: The nous form of the present, minus -ons, plus -ant
The je form of the present, plus -ant
questions.why: Nous parlons gives parlant, nous finissons gives finissant. The only irregulars are ayant, étant and sachant.
Two actions at once by the same subject is the gérondif, and the gérondif always carries en.

questions.q: In « Les gens habitant ici doivent s'inscrire », what is habitant?
questions.why: No en, and it stands in for a relative clause: qui habitent ici. That is the participe présent, and it never agrees.
Here the -ant word simply describes the noun, like an ordinary adjective, so it is an adjectif verbal and it agrees: masculine plural.
Adjectif verbal, feminine singular. Compare « une femme charmant ses invités », where the complement makes it a verb and it stays invariable.

questions.q: Why is there no -e on charmant in « Une femme charmant ses invités » ?
choices: Because charmer has no feminine form
Because it has a complement, so it is a verb and invariable
Because femme is treated as masculine here
questions.why: The complement ses invités is the giveaway: the word is doing verb work, so it is a participe présent. Une femme charmante, with no complement, is an adjective and agrees.

questions.q: Spelling: « un travail (fatiguer) ___ » — an exhausting job.
questions.why: The adjective drops the u: fatigant. The participle keeps it: « ce travail, fatiguant tout le monde, a été abandonné ».

questions.q: Spelling: « le jour (précéder) ___ son départ » — the day preceding his departure.
questions.why: With a complement it is a verb, spelled -ant. Le jour précédent, with -ent, is the adjective meaning the previous day.

questions.q: Which construction can have its own subject, different from the main clause's?
questions.why: « Le train étant en retard, nous avons attendu » — le train is the participle's own subject. A gérondif can only ever refer to the sentence's subject.

questions.q: Build the sentence: People wishing to take part must sign up.
questions.why: The participe présent compresses a relative clause: souhaitant stands for qui souhaitent. It never agrees, however plural the noun.

questions.q: Translate the opening: « ___ mangé, je suis sorti. » — after eating, I went out.
questions.why: French uses the infinitive after prepositions, not -ant. En is the single exception, which is exactly why the gérondif exists.

questions.q: How do you say « Reading is useful » in French?
questions.why: Where English nominalises with -ing, French uses the plain infinitive. Voir, c'est croire — seeing is believing.

questions.say: On apprend en faisant des erreurs.
questions.q: Type what you hear, in correct written French.
a: On apprend en faisant des erreurs.
On apprend en faisant des erreurs
questions.why: Gérondif of manner: this is how you learn. Faisant comes from nous faisons, minus -ons.

questions.q: Say this out loud: Having finished, she went home.
questions.why: Ayant plus a past participle is the participe passé composé, meaning having done. It marks the action as earlier than the main verb.

questions.q: Give the one test that separates the gérondif, the participe présent and the adjectif verbal, with an example of each.
a: Ask what job the word is doing. Is there an en in front? Gérondif, invariable: il travaille en écoutant la radio. Does it have a complement or replace qui plus a verb? Participe présent, invariable: les personnes souhaitant participer. Is it just describing a noun, like big or red? Adjectif verbal, and it agrees: une histoire intéressante.
questions.why: The three forms are spelled the same, so only their function in the sentence tells them apart — and only the adjective ever agrees.
